summary: This document is the March 2020 Final Regulatory Impact Analysis (FRIA) for the SAFE Vehicles Rule, which sets CAFE and CO2 standards for passenger cars and light trucks for model years 2021-2026, jointly by NHTSA and EPA. It explains the statutory basis for the standards, the analysis fleet and modeling approach, and the costs, benefits and net benefits across alternatives, with the preferred alternative (1.5%/year for passenger cars and light trucks) yielding roughly 40.5 mpg and 201 g/mi CO2 in model year 2030. It also includes a July 1, 2020 clarification to Table VII-471 and the table-of-contents and table data.
one_line: Regulatory impact analysis of the 2020 SAFE Vehicles Rule setting CAFE and CO2 fuel economy standards for US model years 2021-2026.
key_facts: The Final Regulatory Impact Analysis for the SAFE Vehicles Rule is dated March 2020 and was updated July 1, 2020 with one Table VII-471 clarification.
NHTSA is revising existing CAFE standards for MY 2021 and finalizing new standards for MYs 2022-2026; EPA is revising CO2 standards for MYs 2021-2025 and finalizing standards for MY 2026.
CAFE standards must be set at the maximum feasible average fuel economy level the Secretary decides manufacturers can achieve in that model year, under 49 U.S.C. 32902.
EPA established CO2 standards under section 202(a) of the Clean Air Act after finding that CO2 endangers public health and welfare, citing 74 FR 66496, 66518 (December 15, 2009).
The analysis fleet covers 2,952 specific model/configurations based on the best information available as of mid-2019 regarding the model year 2017 fleet.

The analysis assumes manufacturers voluntarily supply technologies with a consumer payback of 30 months or less, equating to a willingness to pay for approximately a quarter of available fuel savings.
Under the final standards, EPA projects 201 grams/mile of CO2 and NHTSA projects 40.5 mpg fleet-wide average in model year 2030.
The agencies state real-world CO2 is typically 25 percent higher and real-world fuel economy typically 20 percent lower than compliance values.

Required technology costs would be reduced by $86 to $126 billion over vehicle lifetimes through MY 2029, and per-vehicle consumer prices would be $977 to $1,083 lower on average than under the 2012 standards.
For the CAFE program, fleetwide net benefits vary from $16.1 billion at a 7 percent discount rate to -$13.1 billion at a 3 percent discount rate.
For the CO2 program, fleetwide societal net benefits vary from $6.4 billion at a 7 percent discount rate to -$22.0 billion at a 3 percent discount rate.
The agencies state the net benefits straddle zero and are small relative to technology costs, which range from -$86.3 billion to -$126.0 billion across CAFE and CO2 programs.

The analysis simulates manufacturer compliance through MY 2032, six years beyond the last year of proposed new standards, because some products are on longer design cycles and credits can be carried forward up to five years.
Under the preferred alternative, MY 2030 required MPG is 34.1 for light trucks and 47.7 for passenger cars, and total lifetime fuel savings are 84 billion gallons for CAFE.
EPCA as amended by EISA requires standards for MYs 2021-2030 to be set at the maximum feasible level, while EISA's ratable increase and 35 mpg by MY 2020 requirement applied only to MYs 2011-2020.
NHTSA's CAFE baseline is the augural standards for MYs 2022-2025 and the existing MY 2021 standard; EPA's CO2 baseline is the final MYs 2021-2025 standards.
